headline: Chicago's underground runs on things the city invented (JB rink skating, the pinball and arcade cabinet, a sneaker colorway named after the Bulls) and on thrift racks still full of six titles' worth of gear, which gives a rebuild with no superstar credible lanes far from drill and the street.
summary: Chicago's scenes are inventions, not imports. South Side skaters roll in synchronized JB 'trains' at The Rink on East 87th Street, Chicago companies from Bally and Williams to Midway built the pinball machine and the arcade basketball game (NBA Jam, whose Bulls famously had no Jordan), and the Air Jordan 1 made the Bulls' home whites a sneaker word worldwide, served today by boutiques like Notre and Saint Alfred. The dynasty also filled the thrift racks with Starter pullovers, Champion jerseys and bootleg title tees, feeding a strict vintage culture and a newer rework scene. What is rising in 2025-26 is the scenes that never needed a superstar: JB skating clips spreading on social, pinball and arcade bars, covered skateparks like Logan Boulevard's under the Kennedy, and a Black queer nightlife lineage on the South Side that predates Northalsted's rainbow. Nike can engage rink, arcade, skate, vintage and queer nightlife through paid, credited partners, and should leave drill, gang-nation symbols and street takeovers alone.

insights.title: The team's home whites became a sneaker word
insights.detail: Since 1985 sneakerheads worldwide have called the white, red and black Air Jordan 1 'Chicagos,' and Chicagoans still say 'gym shoes' for any sneaker. The boutique tier (Notre in the West Loop, Saint Alfred and RSVP Gallery on Milwaukee Ave) sells to the most Jordan-saturated customers anywhere.
insights.implication: One more white-red-black 'Chicago' colorway is the one thing this market already owns. Nike Basketball's Bulls product should bring new stories and materials, coordinate with Jordan Brand, and route boutique collaborations through partners with Nike history like Notre.

insights.title: Chicago built the arcade, and NBA Jam's Bulls had no Jordan
insights.detail: Bally, Williams, Gottlieb and Midway made Chicago the capital of pinball and arcade games, and Stern Pinball in Elk Grove Village is still the world's largest pinball maker. Midway made NBA Jam (1993) in Chicago without Jordan, who controlled his own likeness, so its Bulls were Scottie Pippen and Horace Grant; lead designer Mark Turmell, a Pistons fan, later admitted coding the Bulls to miss late shots against Detroit.
insights.implication: Dot-matrix numerals, backglass art and 'heating up' flames give the Bulls a story that needs no superstar, which suits the Giddey-Buzelis-Wilson rebuild. Evoke the language in original art and license any NBA Jam names, sounds or catchphrases.

insights.title: JB skating is the South Side's rink language
insights.detail: Chicago's own rhythm roller-skating style, JB (after James Brown's funk), moves in synchronized 'trains' of skaters doing smooth backward footwork to a mid-tempo groove, and The Rink on East 87th Street is its home floor. Crews dress alike in track suits and custom tees, and the 2020s roller boom carried JB clips far beyond the South Side.
insights.implication: A Bulls track suit cut for skating, co-designed with JB crews who are credited and paid and launched at the rink rather than downtown, would reach a style-setting Black Chicago community that no other market has.

insights.title: Six titles flooded the thrift racks
insights.detail: The 1991-98 dynasty left Chicago full of Starter half-zip pullovers, Champion jerseys, Chalk Line jackets and bootleg 'three-peat' tees, which still surface at Village Discount Outlet, the Maxwell Street Market and Milwaukee Ave vintage shops. Younger Chicagoans now cut and re-sew these pieces into patchwork jackets and reworked hoodies.
insights.implication: Vintage Bulls is the city's thrift currency, so reissues must be archive-exact down to the tag. 'Three-Peat' is Pat Riley's trademark and retired players need licensing, so original silhouettes in aged color are safer than copying old graphics.

insights.title: Skaters won sanctioned concrete, but winter still rules
insights.detail: Chicago skaters now have Park District parks on the lakefront (Wilson in Uptown, Grant in the South Loop) and the skater-backed Logan Boulevard park under the Kennedy Expressway, which stays dry in rain. Uprise Skateshop on Milwaukee Ave anchors the scene, and months of 'Chiberia' push sessions under overpasses and indoors.
insights.implication: A Nike SB x Bulls drop is credible only through local shops and skaters, with money for park upkeep, and it has to be built for Chicago cold: wind-blocking shells, brushed fleece and gloves that keep grip.

insights.title: Queer nightlife runs from Northalsted to South Shore
insights.detail: The North Side's Northalsted strip (renamed from Boystown in 2022) hosts Pride in June and Market Days in August. The city's Black queer lineage, which gave house music its first floor at The Warehouse, lives on in South Side rooms like South Shore's Jeffery Pub and in Chicago's ballroom and kiki scene.
insights.implication: Pride and Market Days product co-designed with South Side Black queer creators and ballroom houses, credited and paid, with proceeds to an LGBTQ+ group they choose, avoids a generic North Side rainbow drop.

places.name: Notre
places.why: A Chicago boutique with a Nike collaboration history (including Dunk Highs) and the closest top-tier sneaker door to the United Center.

places.name: Saint Alfred
places.why: A long-running Wicker Park store at the center of Chicago's release-day sneaker culture.

places.name: Uprise Skateshop
places.why: The core independent shop for Chicago skaters and the right channel for any Nike SB x Bulls product.

places.name: Grant Skatepark
places.neighborhood: South Loop (south end of Grant Park, near Roosevelt Rd)
places.why: Downtown's sanctioned concrete park with a skyline backdrop, a short ride from the United Center.

places.name: Logan Boulevard Skatepark
places.why: A covered, skater-backed park that stays skateable in rain, a sign of the scene's push for year-round space.

places.name: The Rink Fitness Factory
places.why: Home floor of Chicago's JB skating style and its synchronized skate trains.

places.name: Galloping Ghost Arcade
places.why: Billed as the largest video arcade in the US, it is the shrine to the cabinets Chicago companies built.

places.name: Quimby's Bookstore
places.why: Chicago's zine headquarters since the early 1990s and the place the city's self-publishers sell their work.

places.name: Jeffery Pub
places.why: Among the oldest Black-owned gay bars in the country and a living link to the South Side's house-music nightlife.

places.name: Maxwell Street Market
places.why: The city's historic Sunday market, long known for bargains, knockoffs and bootlegs, and a vintage-hunting stop.

people.name: Virgil Abloh (1980-2021)
people.role: Rockford-born designer, RSVP Gallery co-founder with Don C, founder of Off-White
people.why: His Off-White x Nike 'The Ten' included an Air Jordan 1 in Chicago colors, and his 2019 MCA Chicago retrospective 'Figures of Speech' made him the patron saint of Chicago streetwear; his work belongs to his estate and Off-White.

people.name: Notre
people.role: West Loop sneaker and menswear boutique
people.why: Its Nike collaboration history makes it the most natural boutique partner for a Bulls-adjacent drop.

people.name: Saint Alfred
people.why: Sets the release-day agenda for Chicago sneakerheads on Milwaukee Ave.

people.name: Stern Pinball
people.why: The world's largest pinball maker carries on the Bally-Williams-Gottlieb legacy and builds licensed machines, a ready partner for a Bulls arcade story.

people.name: Tim Kitzrow
people.role: Chicago voice actor, the announcer of NBA Jam
people.why: His 'He's on fire!' and 'Boomshakalaka!' calls, recorded for Midway, are arcade-era basketball's most quoted lines and need clearance before any use.

people.name: The Era Footwork Crew
people.why: Battle-tested dancers who perform and teach the city's 160-BPM footwork worldwide, natural wear-testers for a low-top Bulls court shoe.

people.name: Uprise Skateshop
people.why: The scene's trusted retailer, through which Nike SB product and park-upkeep money would read as support rather than sponsorship.

moments.name: Critical Mass Chicago
moments.timing: Last Friday of every month, from Daley Plaza
moments.why: The city's long-running mass bike ride shows how riders customize cold- and night-weather gear.

moments.name: C2E2 (Chicago Comic & Entertainment Expo)
moments.why: The city's biggest comics and pop-culture convention, where gaming and cosplay crowds meet.

moments.name: Chicago Zine Fest
moments.why: The self-publishing scene's annual gathering and a pool of local illustrators for printed inserts and graphics.

moments.name: Anime Central (ACen)
moments.timing: May, Donald E. Stephens Convention Center, Rosemont
moments.why: The Midwest's largest anime convention, where Bulls jerseys are a common base for cosplay mash-ups.

moments.name: Chicago Pride Parade
moments.timing: Last Sunday of June, Lakeview and Northalsted
moments.why: The citywide moment for queer-community product co-designed with South Side and ballroom partners.

moments.name: Northalsted Market Days
moments.why: The Midwest's biggest LGBTQ+ street festival and a late-summer window before Bulls preseason.

moments.name: Mexican Independence Day on 26th Street
moments.timing: Mid-September, Little Village parade and flag-flying car caravans
moments.why: Peak of Chicago's Mexican car and flag culture; support the parade organizers rather than downtown caravan imagery.

moments.name: Pinball Expo
moments.why: The long-running pinball show in pinball's home region lands right at Bulls tip-off, a natural launch for an arcade capsule.

vocabulary.meaning: Chicago's everyday word for any sneakers, used where other cities say 'sneakers' or 'kicks'.
Sneakerhead name for the white, varsity red and black Air Jordan 1, after the Bulls' home whites.
Black-and-red colorway, from the Bulls' road palette on the Air Jordan 1 and 11.
Chicago's rhythm roller-skating style, named after James Brown and skated in synchronized 'trains'.
Chicago's early-2010s party dance and 'bop music' rap wave (Sicko Mobb, DLow), lighter and faster than drill.
The North Side LGBTQ+ district on Halsted St, renamed from 'Boystown' in 2022; using the new name signals respect.
Claiming a shoveled street parking spot with lawn chairs or cones after a snowfall.
The deepest freeze of a Chicago winter, a nickname that took off in the January 2014 cold wave.

designCues.source: Orange plasma dot-matrix score displays on Bally, Williams and Stern pinball machines built in and around Chicago since the early 1990s.
designCues.use: A small accent for numbers and scores on black Bulls shooting shirts and hangtags, next to Bulls red (#CE1141), never a body color.

designCues.source: Pinball score displays and the blocky type on Midway's Chicago-made arcade cabinets.
designCues.use: Build an original dot-grid number and name set for warmups and player tees; don't copy any game's font, logo or sprites.

designCues.source: Sun- and wash-faded red on 1990s Starter and Champion Bulls gear pulled from Village Discount Outlet and Maxwell Street.
designCues.use: Garment-dyed fleece and tees in this red over a sail (#EFE6D3) base, against crisp Bulls red (#CE1141) on game product, so lifestyle reads 'found'.

designCues.source: The satin-and-nylon Bulls pullover with kangaroo pocket and side zip, the city's 1990s winter uniform and today's top vintage find.
designCues.use: Rebuild the silhouette in Nike's own construction (quilted lining, oversized hood, side zip) without Starter's star or other trade dress.

designCues.source: Unofficial dynasty-era championship tees: misregistered colors, slightly-off player art and heavy plastisol ink.
designCues.use: Apply the off-register look to original Bulls graphics on a limited lifestyle tee; never reproduce real bootleg art or 'three-peat' wording.

designCues.source: JB crews at The Rink on 87th dressing alike in fitted track suits for synchronized trains.
designCues.use: Smooth stretch tricot with a tapered, ankle-zip leg that clears skate boots and a blank chest panel for crew-name embroidery.

designCues.cue: The Bulls without Jordan, two-player mode
designCues.source: NBA Jam's 1993 Bulls were Pippen and Horace Grant because Jordan kept his likeness out of the game.
designCues.use: Frame rebuild duo product (Giddey and Buzelis, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson) as a two-player select screen: the Bulls have been cool without a superstar before.

productHooks: Bulls Arcade capsule: black shooting shirt and tee with original dot-grid numerals in display amber (#FF6B1A) and Bulls red (#CE1141), launched around Pinball Expo and the October tip-off at a Chicago arcade, with any NBA Jam references licensed first.
Two-Player Select tees: Giddey/Buzelis and Buzelis/Wilson duo graphics in an original 1990s select-screen layout under the NBPA group license, released for the first home game.

Rink Session track suit: a stretch tricot Bulls jacket and tapered ankle-zip pant cut for skating, co-designed with JB crews from The Rink on 87th, with custom crew-name embroidery and a South Side Bulls skate-night launch where crews are paid.

Basement Stock reissue: a Nike-built half-zip pullover and garment-dyed fleece in aged red (#A8323E) and sail (#EFE6D3), sold only at Chicago doors and the United Center as a nod to the city's thrift hunt.

Chiberia SB pack through Nike SB and Chicago skate shops: a wind-blocking Bulls shell, brushed fleece and grip gloves, with part of the proceeds going to upkeep at Logan Boulevard or Grant skatepark through a group the skaters choose.
Pride and Market Days warm-up co-designed with South Side Black queer creators and Chicago ballroom houses, with credited, paid partners and proceeds to an LGBTQ+ organization they pick.
watchouts: Jordan Brand owns the city's sneaker story: the 'Chicago' Air Jordan 1, the Jumpman and Jordan's name and likeness need Jordan Brand coordination, Virgil Abloh's designs belong to his estate and Off-White, and key locals have rival deals (Joe Freshgoods with New Balance, the Sky's Angel Reese with Reebok).

Chicago street-gang 'nations' use specific symbols: pitchforks, crowns, five- and six-point stars combined with them, hat tilts and certain color pairings. Have local community partners review every graphic; the city flag's six-point stars are fine on their own.

Leave drill, O-Block and the word 'Chiraq' out entirely, along with street takeovers, drifting and dirt-bike or ATV stunts on Lake Shore Drive, which are illegal and a city enforcement priority. Downtown Mexican Independence Day car caravans have drawn police clashes.

Third-party IP: NBA Jam's name, sounds and catchphrases, pinball makers' marks (Stern, Bally, Williams), Starter's star, Pat Riley's 'Three-Peat' trademark and retired players' likenesses all need licensing.

JB skating, footwork, ballroom and South Side house nightlife are Black- and queer-built: partner with, credit and pay their crews and venues, and never brand non-commercial spaces like Critical Mass or skater-built spots.
